title: sendfile() Transfers
description: Transfers files to sockets with sendfile, avoiding userspace copies entirely. Data moves from page cache to the NIC via DMA; the application never touches the bytes. Static file servers live on it.

demo.title: Demo — sendfile() Transfers

title: splice() Pipelines
description: Moves data between file descriptors with splice through kernel pipes, zero-copy. Proxies shuffle bytes from socket to socket without userspace involvement. It is the generic zero-copy plumbing.

demo.title: Demo — splice() Pipelines

title: MSG_ZEROCOPY Sockets
description: Transmits with MSG_ZEROCOPY so the kernel DMaes from userspace buffers. Completion notifications tell the app when buffers are safe to reuse. It brings zero-copy transmit to normal sockets.

demo.title: Demo — MSG_ZEROCOPY Sockets

title: DMA-BUF Sharing
description: Shares DMA buffers between devices with DMA-BUF file descriptors. A camera buffer goes straight to the GPU or NIC without copies; exporters and importers coordinate via fences. It is the Linux zero-copy currency.

demo.title: Demo — DMA-BUF Sharing

title: Page Flipping
description: Flips pages between the network stack and application instead of copying. The receiver's pages become the application's pages; only metadata moves. It is the oldest zero-copy trick, still effective.

demo.title: Demo — Page Flipping

title: PACKET_MMAP Rings
description: Maps kernel packet rings into userspace for zero-copy capture and transmit. The app reads packets straight from the shared ring; no recvmsg copies. Tcpdump-class tools use it.

demo.title: Demo — PACKET_MMAP Rings

title: RDMA Verbs
description: Transfers memory to memory with RDMA verbs, bypassing the remote CPU entirely. One-sided reads and writes move data at line rate with microsecond latency. HPC and NVMe-oF depend on it.

demo.title: Demo — RDMA Verbs

title: io_uring Networking
description: Drives sockets with io_uring submission and completion rings, batching syscalls to near zero. Registered buffers enable true zero-copy; one syscall submits hundreds of operations. It is the modern Linux fast path.

demo.title: Demo — io_uring Networking

title: Buffer Pool Recycling
description: Recycles fixed-size buffers through pools so the fast path never allocates. Allocation is the hidden copy-cost; pools make it disappear. Sizing the pool is the tuning knob.

demo.title: Demo — Buffer Pool Recycling

title: Header/Data Split
description: Splits headers from payloads so headers go to the CPU and payloads DMA to their destination. The NIC separates them on receive; software processes tiny headers while bulk data never moves. SmartNICs do this in hardware.

demo.title: Demo — Header/Data Split

title: Checksum Offload
description: Offloads checksum computation to the NIC so the CPU never touches payload bytes. Touching bytes to checksum them is a hidden copy; offload removes it. Every modern NIC does it.

demo.title: Demo — Checksum Offload

title: Hugepage Packet Buffers
description: Backs packet buffers with huge pages to cut TLB misses on the fast path. At millions of packets per second, TLB misses are measurable; huge pages remove them. DPDK made it standard.

demo.title: Demo — Hugepage Packet Buffers

title: NUMA-Pinned Buffers
description: Pins packet buffers and threads to the same NUMA node as the NIC. Cross-node DMA and access add latency; locality keeps the fast path fast. L3 forwarding benchmarks demand it.
key_mechanisms: Pin threads to the NIC's node

demo.title: Demo — NUMA-Pinned Buffers

title: Buffer Refcounting
description: Shares buffers between pipeline stages with reference counts instead of copying. Cloning a packet bumps a count; the last user frees it. It is zero-copy composition for packet pipelines.

demo.title: Demo — Buffer Refcounting

title: Zero-Copy Fallbacks
description: Falls back to copies gracefully when zero-copy conditions are not met. Small messages, unaligned buffers, and old kernels all need the copy path; the fast path checks and diverts. Correctness first, speed second.

demo.title: Demo — Zero-Copy Fallbacks
